formation.title: The Restoration of Mutapa
formation.text:
The great stone houses of our ancestors stand renewed. From the hilltop enclosures where the Mwenemutapa once held court, the drums sound again across the plateau, calling the provinces to unity. The Shona and Kalanga peoples look to us as the successors of Great Zimbabwe, a kingdom built on gold, iron, and the favor of Mwari.

But the world beyond the plateau presses close. Swahili merchants and Portuguese traders crowd the river towns, hungry for our gold. Their cloth, glass beads, and firearms are useful, but their ambitions are boundless. Do we harness this trade to build something greater than our ancestors imagined? Or do we look inward, to the strength that made Great Zimbabwe possible, the labor of our farmers, the skill of our smiths, and the spiritual authority of the Mwari cult?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Let the gold flow, and let the world come to us.

modifiers.name: Gold of Sofala
modifiers.text: The rivers carry gold and the merchants carry cloth. Through the feiras of Sofala, Sena, and Tete, the wealth of the plateau flows outward to the Indian Ocean, and the knowledge of the world flows back.

options.text: Mwari provides all we need. Our strength is our own.

modifiers.name: Voice of Mwari
modifiers.text: The oracles of the Matobo Hills speak, and the rains come. The Mwenemutapa rules not because foreigners bring trinkets, but because Mwari grants the harvest. The strength of the kingdom lies in its own soil and the spears of its own sons.

advances.name: Dzimba Dzemabwe
advances.text: The mortarless granite architecture of Great Zimbabwe, a building tradition unique in sub-Saharan Africa.

event.title: The Great Enclosure
event.text:
The walls of Great Zimbabwe still stand, mortarless granite, fitted so precisely that not even a blade can pass between the stones. The Great Enclosure, largest ancient structure in sub-Saharan Africa, rises eleven meters high and stretches two hundred and fifty meters around, enclosing the conical tower where the granary of the Mwenemutapa proclaimed his generosity to his people.

These are not mere ruins. They are a statement of what Shona civilization achieved without mortar, without foreign architects, without any technology that was not born of this plateau. The dzimba dzemabwe, the houses of stone, are our declaration that a great civilization rose here, built by our hands, sustained by our labor, and blessed by Mwari.

advances.name: Njanja Iron Smelting
advances.text: The Njanja clan's forced-draught furnace technology, producing high-quality iron tools and weapons.

advances.name: Pfumo Royal Spearmen
advances.text: Elite infantry armed with the pfumo spear and large cowhide shields, forming the backbone of Mutapa armies.

advances.name: Cult of Mwari
advances.text: The worship of Mwari, supreme deity of rain and fertility, whose oracles at the Matobo Hills guide political and agricultural decisions.

advances.name: Alluvial Gold Panning
advances.text: Seasonal gold extraction from riverbeds, families pan for gold after the harvest, feeding the Sofala trade route.

advances.name: Cattle of the Plateau
advances.text: Livestock as the foundation of Shona social hierarchy, cattle are wealth, status, and the currency of bride-price.

advances.name: Plateau Trade Routes
advances.text: Ancient trade paths connecting the Zimbabwe Plateau to the Swahili coast, carrying gold, ivory, and iron.

advances.name: Provincial Governors
advances.text: The dare court system, provincial judges and governors who administer the law and collect tribute on behalf of the Mwenemutapa.

advances.name: Sofala Trade Network
advances.text:
The regulated exchange of gold for cloth, glass beads, and other goods through the Swahili port of Sofala.

Available in: Feira Trading Post

advances.name: Nhare Scouts
advances.text: Swift reconnaissance troops named for the eland, masters of ambush and rapid pursuit across the plateau.

advances.name: Ivory and Cotton Exports
advances.text: The two great exports of the Mutapa kingdom besides gold, ivory and woven cotton cloth. By custom the tusk that touched the ground when an elephant fell was the Mwenemutapa's.

advances.name: Court of the Mwenemutapa
advances.text: The elaborate ceremonial protocol of the Mwenemutapa's court, where provincial chiefs pay tribute and foreigners petition for trade rights.

advances.name: Stone Masonry Tradition
advances.text:
Continuing refinement of the mortarless granite construction techniques inherited from Great Zimbabwe.

Available in: Njanja Forge

advances.name: Portuguese Contact
advances.text: Diplomatic engagement with the Portuguese, who arrived at Sofala in 1505 seeking to monopolize the gold trade.

advances.name: Muzinda Garrisons
advances.text: Permanent garrison forces stationed at each muzinda provincial seat, trained in defensive warfare.

advances.name: Gold Taxation
advances.text: The Mwenemutapa's fifty-percent tariff on all trade goods entering the kingdom, a bold assertion of fiscal sovereignty.

advances.name: Feira Market System
advances.text: Regulated trading posts where gold, ivory, and cloth are exchanged under the Mwenemutapa's oversight.

advances.name: Oracular Network
advances.text: The Mwari cult's network of priests and spirit mediums, serving as both religious authority and political intelligence.

advances.name: Shaft Mining
advances.text: Deeper extraction techniques moving beyond surface panning to follow gold-bearing reef deposits underground.

advances.name: Changamire's Revolt
advances.text: The breakaway of Changamire Dombo and his Rozvi warriors, who expelled the Portuguese and established a new military order.

event.title: The Rozvi Breakaway
event.text:
A prince of the blood, Changamire Dombo, has broken from the Mwenemutapa's court and seized the ancient heartland of Butua by force of arms. His warriors, who call themselves the Rozvi, 'the destroyers', have swept aside both the weakened garrisons of the old kingdom and the Portuguese prazeiros who had grown fat on Zambezi trade. At the Battle of Maungwe, Dombo's forces annihilated a combined Portuguese-Mutapa army, proving that Shona military power need not depend on foreign firearms.

Dombo rules from Khami, near the ruins of Great Zimbabwe itself, and his Rozvi state threatens to eclipse the Mutapa entirely. Yet his success also demonstrates what Shona military discipline can achieve when freed from Portuguese manipulation. The question is whether to channel the Rozvi spirit into permanent military reform or use this crisis to consolidate political authority.

options.text: Embrace the way of the Rozvi warriors.

modifiers.name: Rozvi Warriors
modifiers.text: Changamire Dombo's warrior tradition, the 'destroyers' who expelled the Portuguese from the interior.

options.text: Consolidate the kingdom before the storm passes.

modifiers.name: Rozvi Consolidation
modifiers.text: The political stability that followed Changamire Dombo's reunification of the Shona heartland.

advances.name: Portuguese Resistance
advances.text: The successful defense against Barreto's 1569 invasion, disease, terrain, and Shona determination defeated European arms.

event.title: The Portuguese Invasion
event.text:
In 1561, a Portuguese Jesuit named Goncalo da Silveira converted the Mwenemutapa Nogomo to Christianity, only to be strangled by the king's own guards days later, at the urging of the Muslim merchants who feared Portuguese monopoly. Lisbon used the martyrdom as pretext for a full military invasion. In 1569, Francisco Barreto led a thousand soldiers up the Zambezi, aiming to seize the gold mines of the interior.

They never reached them. Malaria, dysentery, and the sheer hostility of the terrain consumed Barreto's force. The survivors straggled back to the coast, and the Portuguese took their frustrations out on the Swahili traders they could reach, massacring them at Sena and Tete. The Mwenemutapa watched, levied his fifty-percent tariff on the survivors, and extracted a tribute payment from each new Portuguese captain who dared take office in Mozambique.

The invasion has failed, but the foreigners remain. How do we respond?

options.text: Fortify the plateau. Let the land itself be our shield.

modifiers.name: Fortress of Sovereignty
modifiers.text: The plateau itself defends the kingdom, its diseases, distances, and hostile terrain defeat invaders that Shona spears do not.

options.text: Trade with them on our terms. Gold buys more than blood.

modifiers.name: Controlled Commerce
modifiers.text: The Mwenemutapa dictates the terms of trade, extracting tariffs from every merchant who enters the kingdom.

advances.name: Great Cattle Festival
advances.text: Mass ceremonial gatherings where the Mwenemutapa distributes grain and cattle, binding the kingdom through generosity.

advances.name: Machira Cloth Currency
advances.text:
Standardized cotton cloth used as a medium of exchange throughout the kingdom and its trade networks.

Available in: Machira Weavers' House

advances.name: Zambezi Trade Corridor
advances.text:
The Sena-Tete river route as the commercial artery connecting the interior plateau to the coastal ports.

Available in: Zambezi Wharf

advances.name: Provincial Mobilization
advances.text:
The Mwenemutapa's ability to raise 300,000 men from the provinces, a mobilization system rivaling any contemporary African power. The smiths of the plateau forge the spearheads and battle axes that arm it.

Available in: Njanja Forge

advances.name: Rozvi Ascendancy
advances.text: The military reforms of the Changamire dynasty, which produced disciplined infantry capable of defeating European-armed forces.

advances.name: Firearms Adoption
advances.text: Shona troops armed with Portuguese-acquired muskets, integrating firearms into traditional battlefield tactics.

advances.name: Matopos Spiritual Center
advances.text: The Matobo Hills as the enduring seat of the Mwari cult, a sacred landscape of caves, rock art, and oracular shrines.

advances.name: Ivory Trade Expansion
advances.text: Industrial-scale ivory processing and export to European and Indian Ocean markets.

advances.name: Khami Architecture
advances.text: The distinctive walling style of Khami, capital of the Rozvi, decorative stone courses built upon natural granite platforms.

advances.name: Gold Export Monopoly
advances.text:
Royal control over all gold leaving the kingdom, no merchant trades without the Mwenemutapa's permission. The gold that stays is drawn into wire and beaten into beads by the court's own smiths.

Available in: Njanja Forge

advances.name: Shona Cultural Resilience
advances.text: The survival of Shona identity through Nguni invasions, Portuguese interference, and colonial pressure.

advances.name: Modern Governance
advances.text: Centralized administrative reform for a new era, adapting the dare system to modern state requirements.

advances.name: Anti-Colonial Resistance
advances.text: Organized military opposition to foreign domination, drawing on centuries of Shona martial tradition.

advances.name: Mineral Sovereignty
advances.text: Asserting national control over the Zimbabwe Plateau's gold, copper, and iron wealth.

advances.name: Chimurenga Spirit
advances.text: The enduring Shona tradition of armed resistance against oppression, chimurenga means 'revolutionary struggle.'

advances.name: Pan-Shona Unity
advances.text: Cultural consolidation across Kalanga, Korekore, Zezuru, Manyika, and Ndau peoples under a shared Shona identity.

destiny.name: Destiny of the Mutapa
destiny.text: The drums of formation have sounded and the Mwenemutapa sits enthroned once more. Now the kingdom must prove itself worthy of its ancestors' legacy. Achieve stability and the path forward will reveal itself.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Mutapa Restored
event.text:
The stone walls of our ancestors stand renewed, and the provinces answer to one Mwenemutapa once more. The kingdom that built Great Zimbabwe has risen again, but rising is only the beginning. The world watches to see what we will become.

Will we reach outward, to the ocean routes that carry gold to distant lands? Or will we turn the strength of our spears upon the peoples beyond our borders, building an empire that dwarfs anything our forebears imagined? The choice has been made. Now comes the work.

destiny.name: The Kilwa Connection
destiny.text: Kilwa Kisiwani is the jewel of the Swahili coast, the greatest trading city south of Mombasa. To control it is to hold the key to the Indian Ocean gold trade. Seize Kilwa and accumulate the wealth to prove Mutapa's commercial power.

conditions.text: Chose Gold of Sofala
Own Kilwa, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 1000

event.title: Gold for the Merchants of Kilwa
event.text:
Kilwa Kisiwani, the island city of coral stone and gold, has long been the gateway through which the wealth of the interior reaches the wider world. For centuries, Swahili merchants carried Mutapa's gold northward through Kilwa's harbors to Arabia, India, and beyond. Now that gateway is ours.

With Kilwa under Mutapa's control, the middlemen have become our subjects. Gold dust no longer changes hands three times before reaching a ship; it flows directly from the mines of the plateau to the dhows of the Indian Ocean. The profits that once enriched Swahili sultans now fill the Mwenemutapa's treasury.

options.text: The gold flows on our terms now.

destiny.name: Zanzibar and the Zambezi
destiny.text: With Kilwa secured, the trade network must extend both northward to Zanzibar and inland through the Zambezi corridor. Control these routes and amass wealth to become the undisputed commercial power of southeastern Africa.

conditions.text: Own Zanzibar, or a subject owns it
Own Quelimane, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 2000

event.title: Masters of the Eastern Seaboard
event.text:
From Quelimane on the Zambezi delta to the spice island of Zanzibar, the eastern coast of Africa answers to the Mwenemutapa. The Swahili trading cities, once independent, now operate within a Mutapa-dominated commercial sphere. Ships from Gujarat, Oman, and the Malabar Coast dock at ports where Shona officials collect duties.

This unprecedented maritime reach raises a question: do we partner with the established Swahili merchant class, leveraging their centuries of Indian Ocean expertise? Or do we impose Mutapa's monopoly directly, ensuring that every cowrie shell of profit flows to the royal treasury?

modifiers.name: Swahili Partnership
modifiers.text: A partnership with the established Swahili merchant class, leveraging their Indian Ocean expertise to expand Mutapa's commercial reach.

options.text: The Mwenemutapa takes his rightful share.

modifiers.name: Mutapa Trade Monopoly
modifiers.text: The Mwenemutapa's direct monopoly over coastal trade, enforced by naval patrols and port officials.

destiny.name: Emporium of the South
destiny.text: The final step: Mombasa, the great northern port, must fall under Mutapa's influence. With porcelain flowing through your markets and gold in your treasury, you will have built a trade empire stretching from the plateau to the Indian Ocean.

conditions.text: Own Mombasa, or a subject owns it
A market the country is in

children.text: Porcelain is produced in the market
Porcelain is traded in the market

conditions.text: Gold at least 3000
Prestige at least 75

event.title: The Golden Arc
event.text:
From the deep mines of the Zimbabwe Plateau, through the river corridors and coastal ports, to the great harbor of Mombasa, the golden arc is complete. Mutapa has achieved what no African state south of Egypt has accomplished: a commercial empire spanning from the continental interior to the Indian Ocean.

Porcelain from China graces the Mwenemutapa's table. Silk from Gujarat adorns his court. Gold from a hundred mines pays for it all. The question now is how to sustain this wealth across generations. Do we invest in the trade infrastructure that made this possible, creating a permanent commercial machine? Or do we use this wealth to transform the court itself into a center of learning and cosmopolitan culture?

options.text: Build the golden arc to last forever.

modifiers.name: The Golden Arc
modifiers.text: The complete trade route from plateau mines to Indian Ocean ports, generating wealth that gives Mutapa unmatched negotiating power.

options.text: Let the wealth transform our civilization.

modifiers.name: Cosmopolitan Court
modifiers.text: A court enriched by Indian Ocean trade, drawing foreign artisans, scholars, and soldiers to the Mwenemutapa's service.

destiny.name: The Southern March
destiny.text: The lands south of the Limpopo, the Swazi highlands and the Tswana territories, have long been beyond Mutapa's reach. The road south crosses the Limpopo at Mapungubwe, the hill of the first kings. Mapungubwe, Mapulana and Bakgatla are to be held, and with them the frontier of a greater Shona empire.

conditions.text: Chose Voice of Mwari
Own Mapulana, or a subject owns it
Own Bakgatla, or a subject owns it
Own Mapungubwe, or a subject owns it

event.title: Spears South of the Limpopo
event.text:
The Mwenemutapa's armies have crossed the Limpopo and marched into the lands beyond, territories that were never part of the old Mutapa kingdom. The Swazi highlands and the Tswana chieftaincies have fallen before Shona spears, and new provincial governors take their seats in conquered muzinda.

This is something new. The old Mutapa kingdom was a plateau state, defined by the granite kopjes and gold-bearing rivers of Zimbabwe. Now we are becoming something larger, an empire that absorbs peoples who do not speak Shona, who do not worship Mwari, who have their own traditions of governance. The challenge of ruling them has only just begun.

destiny.name: Conquest of the Highveld
destiny.text: Push deeper into the southern interior. The Kweneng cattle lands and the gold-bearing fields of Lejweleputswa lie waiting. Half of the Thaba Bosiu country is to be held, and Kweneng is to grow into a royal town, for land is kept from the town that rules it.

conditions.text: Own Kweneng, or a subject owns it
Own Lejweleputswa, or a subject owns it
We own Kweneng and it has become a town or a city
We or our non-sovereign subjects hold at least 50% of the locations in the Thaba Bosiu area

event.title: Lords of the Highveld
event.text:
The great grasslands of the interior, the Highveld, are ours. From the cattle-rich plains of Kweneng to the gold-bearing fields of Lejweleputswa, Mutapa's dominion now stretches far beyond anything the founders of Great Zimbabwe could have imagined. The development of these conquered territories has begun in earnest.

But governing distant provinces requires choices. Do we plant garrison settlements of Shona soldiers in every conquered territory, creating permanent military colonies that will hold the frontier? Or do we extract tribute from existing local chiefs, governing through subordinates who know the land?

options.text: Plant garrisons across the conquered lands.

modifiers.name: Settler Garrisons
modifiers.text: Shona military colonies planted across conquered territories, holding the frontier through permanent armed presence.

options.text: Rule through tribute and local authority.

modifiers.name: Tribute Provinces
modifiers.text: Conquered territories governed through local chiefs who pay tribute to the Mwenemutapa, preserving existing structures under Shona overlordship.

destiny.name: Imperium of the Plateau
destiny.text: The ultimate ambition: extend Shona dominion to the western desert frontier at Damara. With stone enclosures or royal granaries raised in three towns, high prestige, and Great Zimbabwe built up to 12 development, the Mwenemutapa will rule the greatest state southern Africa has ever seen.

conditions.text: Own Damara, or a subject owns it
A Dzimba Dzemabwe or a granary stands in at least 3 of our locations
Prestige at least 75
We own Great Zimbabwe and its development is at least 12

event.title: The Imperium Fulfilled
event.text:
From the Indian Ocean coast to the desert frontier, from the Zambezi to the Highveld, the Mwenemutapa rules an empire vaster than any that has risen in southern Africa. The mustering grounds of the capital host armies that would give any European colonial power pause. The prestige of the Shona dynasty echoes across the continent.

This is the moment of choice that defines all empires at their zenith. Do we commit to the warrior-king tradition, the Changamire legacy of military strength that keeps the empire intact through force of arms? Or do we invest in the eternal stones, the building tradition that outlasted every dynasty, the monuments that will speak for Shona civilization long after armies are dust?

modifiers.name: Warrior-Kings
modifiers.text: The Changamire tradition of military supremacy, the empire held together by the sword and the Mwenemutapa's personal prowess in war.

options.text: The stones will speak for us.

modifiers.name: Eternal Stones
modifiers.text: The building tradition of Great Zimbabwe endures, monuments in stone that outlast dynasties and proclaim Shona civilization to the ages.

units.name: Pfumo Spearmen
units.text: Elite Shona infantry armed with the pfumo spear and large cowhide shields. These royal troops form the disciplined core of Mutapa armies, trained in close-order defensive formations.

units.name: Nhare Scouts
units.text: Swift reconnaissance troops named for the eland. Masters of ambush and rapid pursuit, they screen the army's advance and harry retreating foes across the plateau.

units.name: Muzinda Garrison
units.text: Provincial fortress troops drawn from the muzinda administrative seats. Trained in defensive warfare and siege resistance, they hold the stone-walled strongpoints of the kingdom.

units.name: Rozvi Warriors
units.text: Shock infantry of the Changamire dynasty. The Rozvi, 'the destroyers', are aggressive offensive troops who proved at the Battle of Maungwe that Shona arms could defeat Portuguese muskets.

units.name: Mutapa Musketmen
units.text: Shona soldiers armed with Portuguese-acquired firearms. These troops combine European weapons technology with Mutapa battlefield discipline.

buildings.name: Dzimba Dzemabwe
buildings.text: Great stone enclosures in the Zimbabwe tradition, mortarless granite walls fitted with such precision that a blade cannot pass between the stones. These serve as royal courts, granaries, and symbols of Shona civilization.

buildings.name: Dare Court
buildings.text: The royal judicial court where provincial governors administer justice, collect tribute, and maintain the Mwenemutapa's authority over the kingdom's districts.

buildings.name: Njanja Forge
buildings.text: Advanced Shona iron smelting works. The Njanja clan builds batteries of forced-draught furnaces, each with paired bellows and rear tuyere holes, producing iron of exceptional quality for tools and weapons.

buildings.name: Mwari Shrine
buildings.text: A sacred oracular site dedicated to Mwari, supreme deity of rain, fertility, and the harvest. Priests interpret the voice of Mwari from cave echoes and pronounce blessings or curses upon the land.

buildings.name: Feira Trading Post
buildings.text: A regulated trading market where gold dust from the plateau meets cloth, glass beads, and porcelain from the Indian Ocean trade. The Mwenemutapa's agents oversee every exchange.

buildings.name: Alluvial Gold Works
buildings.text: Organized gold panning and washing along the riverbanks. Families work the alluvial deposits after the harvest season, and every sluice raises what the gold country yields to the kingdom's export trade.

where.text: The location's raw material is Gold

buildings.name: Kraal Stockade
buildings.text: A fortified cattle compound serving as a provincial defensive strongpoint. The thick wooden stockade shelters livestock and provides a rallying point for local militia against invaders.

buildings.name: Zambezi Wharf
buildings.text: A river trading post along the Zambezi corridor, facilitating the movement of gold, ivory, and imported goods between the plateau and the coast.

buildings.name: Royal Cattle Post
buildings.text: A post of the king's herds in cattle country. The beasts graze the long grass of the plateau in the rains and are driven down to the lowveld in the dry season, and the herders of the post raise more cattle from the same pasture.

where.text: The location's raw material is Livestock

buildings.name: Elephant Hunters' Camp
buildings.text: A camp of elephant hunters in ivory country. The tusk that touches the ground when the elephant falls is owed to the Mwenemutapa; the other is the hunter's to sell.

where.text: The location's raw material is Ivory

buildings.name: Indian Ocean Emporium
buildings.text: The apex of Mutapa's commercial ambitions, a great trading house where goods from China, India, Arabia, and the African interior converge under the Mwenemutapa's authority.

buildings.name: Royal Mustering Ground
buildings.text: The central parade ground where the Mwenemutapa reviews his armies. Rozvi warriors, Pfumo spearmen, and musketmen drill side by side beneath the royal standard.

buildings.name: Machira Weavers' House
buildings.text: Weavers of machira, the cotton cloth of the Zambezi valley and the plateau, whose cloths passed from hand to hand as a measure of value.

list.name: Mhondoro Oracular Network
list.text: The mhondoro were the spirit-mediums of royal ancestors, possessed by deceased Mwene Mutapas to speak through living svikiro. From the great shrines of Matonjeni and the Matopos, oracular pronouncements legitimized the king's decrees, set rainmaking calendars, and confirmed succession. The institution bound the monarchy to a parallel sacred administration; lineage chiefs who tried to consult their own ancestors found the royal mhondoro speaking louder.

conditions.text: Any of

list.name: Kuronzera Cattle Clientship
list.text: Under the kuronzera system the Mwene Mutapa loaned royal cattle to commoners and lesser chiefs, who in return owed labor, military service, and a share of calves. The herds threaded the realm with thousands of personal bonds running directly to the throne, bypassing hereditary lineage authority. Drought, rinderpest, or royal greed could collapse the network overnight, scattering clients back to their old chiefs.

list.name: Curva Annual Tribute
list.text: Each year the Mwene Mutapa held the curva, a ceremony at which vassal chiefs and their headmen brought ivory, gold, hoes, and cloth to renew their oath of submission. The Portuguese chronicler Joao dos Santos described the rite in 1609 as the central event of imperial calendar: absence from curva was treated as rebellion. The king redistributed gifts to bind chiefs back into the hierarchy, but the burden of tribute fell heaviest on the cultivators below them.

list.name: Mukomohasha Captaincy
list.text: The mukomohasha was the supreme captain of the Mwene Mutapa's armies, an office filled by appointment rather than inheritance and held distinct from the great lineage chiefs. Portuguese sources from the late sixteenth century describe him riding at the head of the royal host with subordinate captains drawn from across the realm. The captaincy gave the throne a permanent military arm independent of the kraals, and the cultivators who provisioned the marching column.
